title: Extreme-ultraviolet lithography into high-volume chip manufacturing
sourceNativeSummary: EUV required a long coupled development across source power, optics, masks, resist, metrology, contamination control and scanner reliability. ASML records 2019 as the point when EUV entered high-volume manufacturing fabs.
rivalOrBoundary: A physics-capable exposure tool became industrially useful only after throughput, uptime, yield and customer-fab integration crossed a manufacturing threshold.
pressure: EUV promised much shorter-wavelength lithography for continued chip scaling, but laboratory exposure was not sufficient: source power, reflective optics, masks, resist, vacuum, contamination control, metrology, uptime and wafer throughput all had to work together inside production fabs.
preExistingWorldModel: EUV development had lasted roughly two decades. Prototype/early-production scanners existed before 2019, but customers needed productivity and availability high enough for high-volume manufacturing rather than isolated patterning demonstrations.
candidateRoutes: continue multi-patterning with mature deep-ultraviolet lithography
introduce EUV only for a narrow subset of critical layers
push EUV source power, optics, masks/resist and scanner reliability toward high-volume manufacturing
delay EUV until next-generation High-NA systems
observationsAndInstruments: ASML reports that EUV progressed into high-volume manufacturing of commercial microchips after a roughly 20-year development journey.
In 2019 EUV systems entered high-volume manufacturing fabs.

NXE:3400C increased throughput from about 125 to 170 wafers per hour and demonstrated over 2,000 wafers per day under customer DRAM conditions, while availability/productivity improvements reduced production cost per wafer.
decisiveTests: can 13.5 nm EUV exposure achieve required pattern fidelity
can source/optics/mask/resist contamination and defect control meet production needs
can scanner availability and wafers-per-hour cross a fab-economic threshold
can metrology/process control and customer process integration sustain yield
technicalOrScientificTransition: EUV moved from physically capable exposure to a coupled manufacturing platform whose throughput, availability, yield and customer integration made the shorter wavelength economically usable at scale.
complements: customer process integration and supply network
rivalsAndFailures: Mature DUV multi-patterning remained a viable rival and dominated shipment volume even as EUV entered HVM.
EUV could have remained technically impressive but economically unusable if availability/throughput/yield failed to mature.
diffusionAndScaling: Customer introduction of EUV-manufactured devices and HVM fab deployment turned EUV into a production substrate for leading-edge logic/memory.
standardsAndInstitutions: ASML, customers, optics suppliers, materials suppliers and research partners co-developed the system; no single component owner could unilaterally establish production standing.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Resolution, throughput, availability, yield, energy use, tool cost and supply-chain concentration are distinct system dimensions.
secondOrderEffects: Once conventional EUV entered production, frontier pressure shifted toward higher numerical aperture, metrology/inspection, resist/mask challenges and continued cost/productivity improvement.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: Which complement was rate-limiting at each stage of EUV maturation?
How much of HVM crossing depended on scanner improvement versus customer process adaptation?
